lesson.title: Zijn & Have Gym
lesson.subtitle: ben/bent/is, heb/hebt/heeft — identity, possession and hunger

hook.title: Four Frames, One Verb Pair
hook.content: Identity, location, possession and bodily states all run through zijn and hebben. Ik ben hier, ik heb honger, het is koud: the frame changes, the verbs do not.

pattern.title: Choose the frame, then the verb
pattern.content: Being: ik ben, het is. Possession and bodily states: ik heb honger, ik heb dorst. Weather: het is koud. The noun after hebben is the thing you 'have'.
pattern.trap_note: English 'I am cold' is usually ik heb het koud, not ik ben koud. The body feels cold through hebben.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Zijn & Have Gym):
exercises.target_answer: zijn, hebben, de honger, de dorst, koud, warm
exercises.meaning: to be, to have, hunger, thirst, cold, warm
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Zijn & Have Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Het is koud.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Zijn & Have Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Choose the frame, then the verb
exercises.explanation: “Wij hebben dorst.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Choose the frame, then the verb.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: English 'I am cold' is usually ik heb het koud, not ik ben koud. The body feels cold through hebben.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Hij heeft honger.” is word-for-word “He has hunger.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Choose the frame, then the verb.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Het is warm.” reuses only material taught in “Zijn & Have Gym” — Choose the frame, then the verb.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het is warm.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Choose the frame, then the verb.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “You are not thirsty.”
twist.explanation: Geen negates the indefinite noun dorst; hebben stays the frame.

summary.outcome: Swap between zijn and hebben for identity, weather and bodily states.
summary.takeaway: Dutch often says you 'have' a state English says you 'are'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: De & Het: Gender Without Case.

zijn.etymology_derivation: The being verb is irregular in every Germanic language; English is and Dutch is are the same old root.

hebben.etymology_derivation: English have and Dutch hebben descend from the same verb; the b is preserved.

honger.etymology_derivation: English hunger and Dutch honger are the same word; Dutch says 'have hunger'.

dorst.etymology_derivation: English thirst and Dutch dorst are the same word; Dutch says 'have thirst'.

koud.etymology_derivation: English cold and Dutch koud are the same word.

warm.etymology_derivation: The same word as English warm.
